note: Hand-computed label positions. Every `at` here was worked out on paper from the path's own definition, NOT read off a run of the engine, and no oracle fixture generator writes this file. That is the point of it: the numbers are a second source of truth, and a port that got the unit wrong disagrees with them for reasons no amount of self-consistency would hide.
unit: `labelPosition` is a FRACTION of the path's total arc length, `targetLength = clamp(f, 0, 1) * totalLength` (linearElementEditor.ts@1118751f:2050). A fraction and a world-unit offset are indistinguishable on a straight horizontal line and disagree on everything else, so the cases below are built to disagree.

cases.name: a right angle, three points, sharp
cases.why: Chords of 120 and 90, so the path is 210 long. Three ways of reading the same number that a test must not confuse: a fraction of the bounding box (120 x 90), a fraction of each segment, and a world-unit offset. At 0.25 the answers are (52.5, 0) for a fraction of the length, (30, 0) for a box x-fraction, (30, 0) for a per-segment fraction, and (0.25, 0) for an offset. 0.6 puts the answer 6 into the SECOND chord, which a per-segment fraction could never reach.

cases.name: one straight run, three hundred long, sharp
cases.why: A two-point path is drawn as a single cubic whose controls sit on the chord, so the curve IS the straight line and every fraction is exactly `a + f * (b - a)`. 0.25 of 300 is 75, not 0.25 and not 0.25 of the box by accident.

cases.name: one straight run, three hundred long, rounded
cases.why: The SAME expected points as the sharp case above, and that is the finding rather than a copy: with two points a Catmull-Rom spline is the straight run through them, so `roundness` cannot move a label on a two-point path. A port that rounded a straight run into something else fails here.

cases.name: the same straight run, turned a quarter
cases.why: Points [[0,0],[300,0]] at x=y=0, turned by pi/2 about the centre of the points, which is (150, 0). The world path is therefore the VERTICAL run from (150, -150) to (150, 150), and 0.25 of it is (150, -75). A port that measured in the element's own unrotated frame answers (75, 0) — on the ghost of the path, which is the bug this whole task is about for a curved arrow, arriving here by another road.

cases.name: a symmetric arch, three points, rounded
cases.why: The Catmull-Rom control points, worked out by hand from the duplicated ends: the first cubic is [(0,0), (50/3,50/3), (200/3,100), (100,100)] and the second is its mirror in x = 100. Two equal halves, so half the arc length is exactly where they meet, which is the middle point (100, 100). The other fractions need the arc length of a cubic and are NOT here; the bowed case is cross-checked against a second implementation instead, because a hand-waved integration constant is a magic number wearing a lab coat.
